tldr: To train vision models for underwater robots, researchers extended the IsaacSim-based marine simulator "OceanSim" with a synthetic data generation pipeline that automatically generates high-quality labeled data at scale. Tested on a real-world sea urchin detection task, the study reveals how variations in haze, terrain, and distractors affect sim-to-real transfer and highlights current challenges.
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed Synthetic Data Generation (SDG) pipeline. Starting from placing target objects on a noise plane, adding PBR terrain, populating distractors (such as seaweeds and shells), and applying underwater haze effects, the pipeline automatically synthesizes photorealistic images close to real-world marine data from the SeaClear dataset (far right).
overview:
The biggest bottleneck in underwater robot vision is the severe lack of labeled real-world data. Marine data collection is remarkably costly and labor-intensive. Moreover, scene appearance shifts drastically depending on location, depth, and turbidity. This causes a severe domain shift: models trained on data from one sea area often fail completely when deployed in another.

To tackle this challenge, the authors turned to Synthetic Data Generation (SDG). They extended OceanSim, an IsaacSim-based underwater simulator, to build a pipeline that automatically generates massive amounts of labeled synthetic images. The pipeline integrates physically based realistic terrain, 3D object assets created via generative models, and fast deferred shading that mimics underwater light attenuation and backscattering (haze effects). They also implemented a ROS2 wrapper to ease integration with physical robots.

Using a sea urchin detection task from the real-world SeaClear benchmark dataset, they evaluated object detection models (CNN-based YOLOv9 and Transformer-based DETR) trained purely on simulator imagery. The results demonstrated that zero-shot detection on real images is feasible using synthetic images alone, and that different model architectures benefit from different types of randomization (appearance-based haze vs. structural terrain). However, simply scaling up the number of synthetic images yielded diminishing returns, particularly in recall for distant, hazy objects. This highlighted sim-to-real barriers in the fidelity of simplified underwater light transport models and the diversity of 3D assets.
contributions: Implemented a synthetic data generation (SDG) pipeline inside the IsaacSim-based underwater simulator OceanSim, automatically integrating underwater optical models (haze), PBR terrain, and distractors.
Developed and open-sourced a ROS2 wrapper to facilitate underwater sensor data acquisition and robot control directly from the simulator.

Quantitatively evaluated sim-to-real transfer performance and the impact of individual domain randomization components using purely simulation-trained models on a real-world sea urchin detection task (SeaClear).

Identified key drivers of the underwater sim-to-real gap that cannot be bridged simply by increasing synthetic image count (e.g., simplified light transport models and limited asset diversity), laying out a roadmap for future marine perception research.

sections.heading: Why is real underwater data so scarce, and why do we need synthetic data?
sections.summary: Underwater environments suffer from severe light absorption, scattering, and fluctuating turbidity, making large-scale dataset collection prohibitively expensive. This section explains the motivation behind introducing a synthetic data generation pipeline and ROS2 integration to OceanSim to address this bottleneck.
sections.details:
In underwater robotics perception, the primary bottlenecks are the scarcity of real-world training data and severe environmental degradation. Light undergoes wavelength-dependent attenuation and backscattering from suspended particles, combined with heavy shifts in turbidity and illumination. Consequently, scene appearance changes drastically depending on location, depth, and sensor setups. As a result, models trained on data gathered with great effort in one marine site suffer catastrophic performance drops when moved to another.

A promising approach to resolve this issue is Synthetic Data Generation (SDG). Simulation allows for cost-effective, scalable generation of annotated data without being bounded by field accessibility or hardware constraints. However, synthesizing datasets that realistically capture underwater visual phenomena remains difficult.

OceanSim, an existing IsaacSim-based underwater perception simulator, provides a platform for fast, high-fidelity marine rendering. Yet, it lacked a systematic framework to mass-produce labeled training data for machine learning. In this work, the authors extended OceanSim to build a highly configurable SDG pipeline and introduced a ROS2 wrapper for seamless integration with downstream robot applications. By testing purely simulation-trained object detection models on a real-world marine task, this study thoroughly examines the current state and limitations of underwater sim-to-real transfer.

sections.heading: What are current underwater simulators missing, and how should underwater light be modeled?
sections.summary: This section reviews terrestrial synthetic data generation and existing underwater simulators to identify key gaps. It also introduces marine optics theory (the Sea-thru model) used to capture underwater light attenuation and backscattering.
sections.details:
This section reviews related work across three main perspectives: synthetic data for perception, underwater simulators, and underwater rendering.

### II-A Synthetic Data for Perception
In terrestrial settings, synthetic data has long been used as a replacement for real data or for pretraining. Recently, scalable pipelines that automatically generate rich labels including segmentation, depth, and bounding boxes have gained traction. However, simple domain randomization techniques popular on land (randomizing colors and textures) often fail in underwater environments due to their unique optical characteristics.

### II-B Underwater Simulators
Several underwater simulators exist, such as Stonefish, HoloOcean, UNav-Sim, and Aqua-Verse. However, most focus heavily on dynamics or specific sensors (such as sonar), lacking dedicated SDG pipelines for systematically generating large-scale labeled training datasets. OceanSim bridges this gap by combining fast physics-based rendering with a flexible SDG framework.

### II-C Underwater Rendering
Underwater image degradation is driven by wavelength-dependent absorption and scattering. Directly solving the radiative transfer equation is computationally prohibitive and unsuitable for real-time simulation. Therefore, this work adopts a practical optical model based on research by Akkaynak et al. and "Sea-thru," which decomposes light into direct transmission and backscatter while applying scene-depth-dependent attenuation.

sections.heading: How do you recreate underwater realism? Combining procedural generation with optical effects
sections.summary: This section describes the automated data generation pipeline built on OpenUSD and IsaacSim physics, integrating terrain, targets, distractors, and haze effects. It introduces a deferred shading optical model for real-time performance and an intuitive GUI playground.
sections.details:
The proposed SDG pipeline takes target 3D meshes, background distractor meshes, and scanned natural terrain meshes as inputs. Using the OpenUSD API and the IsaacSim physics engine, object placements and camera poses are procedurally randomized to automatically export KITTI-format labeled images.

### III-A Haze (Underwater Optical Model)
To reproduce underwater image formation, the pipeline implements a model based on Sea-thru via deferred shading, decoupling geometric rendering from optical post-processing. For each RGB channel $c$, the observed image $I_c$ is modeled as:
$$I_{c} = J_{c}e^{-\beta_{\text{attn},c}d} + B_{\infty,c}\left(1-e^{-\beta_{\text{bs},c}d}\right)$$
where $J_c$ is the clear in-air image rendered by IsaacSim, $d$ is camera distance (depth map), $\beta_{\text{attn},c}$ is the attenuation coefficient, $\beta_{\text{bs},c}$ is the backscatter coefficient, and $B_{\infty,c}$ is the veiling light (water color at infinity). The first term represents direct transmission attenuating over distance, while the second term accounts for backscattering from particles suspended in the water column. While slightly less physically faithful than volumetric rendering, it allows fast, real-time generation of underwater imagery.

### III-B Terrain
Real-world scanned PBR (Physically Based Rendering) textures sourced from PolyHaven are applied to IsaacSim's OmniPBR materials. Because the haze model depends heavily on accurate depth, displacement maps are used to physically deform flat plane meshes into uneven, realistic seabed terrains.

### III-C Objects and Distractors
To mimic the real-world SeaClear dataset, 3D sea urchin assets were created using image-to-3D generative models like SAM3D and Hyper3D. In addition, non-target distractor assets such as seaweeds, shells, and corals were collected from SketchFab and pooled together to inject natural visual complexity into the scene.

### III-D Domain Randomization and GUI Playground
Four workspaces are defined: target objects, distractors, camera position, and camera look-at point. Positions and poses are uniformly sampled within these bounds. Random scale and bias shifts are applied to asset textures to encourage color diversity. An intuitive GUI playground is also provided, allowing users to interactively tune and inspect these complex parameter configurations.

captions.F3: The GUI playground built inside IsaacSim for configuring synthetic data generation. The left panel allows tuning sampling bounds for objects, camera positions, and texture variations, while the right viewport provides interactive visualization of 3D bounding boxes.

sections.heading: Direct robot integration: A ROS2 wrapper handling sensor streams and controls
sections.summary: A ROS2 wrapper was developed to bridge the simulator with external robotics software stacks. It streams various underwater sensor topics and enables direct velocity control of the simulated vehicle.
sections.details:
Robotics research relies heavily on the ROS ecosystem. In this pipeline, a wrapper was implemented to ensure seamless communication between the IsaacSim environment and ROS2 nodes.

Standard ROS2 topics are defined for all sensors supported by OceanSim. The wrapper publishes RGB images, depth images, segmentation masks, and camera intrinsics (CameraInfo), as well as typical underwater robotic sensors such as IMUs, DVLs (Doppler Velocity Logs), and acoustic sensors.

Furthermore, direct velocity commands can be sent to the simulated ego-robot via the `cmd_vel` topic. This allows the simulator to serve not only for generating perception training data, but also for immediate closed-loop simulation and autonomous navigation testing using the trained perception models.

sections.heading: Spotting real-world sea urchins: Testing sim-to-real transfer with pure simulation training
sections.summary: Object detection models trained solely on synthetic imagery were evaluated zero-shot on the real-world SeaClear dataset. The study reveals behavioral differences between CNNs (YOLOv9) and Transformers (DETR), the impact of each randomization factor, and dataset scale effects.
sections.details:
### V-A Experimental Setup and Synthetic Dataset Generation
As a real-world benchmark, the single-class detection of sea urchins—rigid objects with relatively simple geometries—was chosen. Five sea urchin models, 30 natural terrain assets (sand, pebbles, rock faces), and 30 distractor assets (corals, seaweeds, shells) were prepared to generate labeled synthetic datasets in OceanSim. The baseline $1\times$ dataset consisted of 1,800 images.

### V-B Model Training and Evaluation
Two architectures were trained: the CNN-based YOLOv9 and the Transformer-based DETR-ResNet50. Both were trained for 100 epochs using identical preprocessing and data augmentations. The real-world test set comprised 179 images containing 718 annotated sea urchins from the SeaClear dataset. Models were evaluated using $\mathrm{mAP}_{50}$, $\mathrm{mAP}_{50\text{-}95}$, and Precision and Recall at maximum F1 score.

### V-C Sim-to-Real Performance and Ablations
Ablation experiments revealed intriguing differences based on model architecture:
- **Importance of haze**: Models trained without haze failed to detect sea urchins that blended into the background due to attenuation and backscatter, causing a high rate of false negatives (misses).
- **Architectural differences**: YOLOv9 (CNN) is sensitive to local pixel-level appearance, making the presence of haze crucial. In contrast, DETR benefited more strongly from terrain diversity, capturing global structures such as textures and occlusions.
- **Role of distractors**: Distractors encourage structural generalization. However, adding them without haze or realistic terrain increased domain shift too much; they only proved effective when combined with other realistic factors.

### Comparison with Real-Data Baselines and Remaining Challenges
Scaling synthetic data fivefold ($5\times$, 9,000 images) yielded only marginal improvements in $\mathrm{mAP}_{50}$ for DETR. When compared against a baseline trained on 1,800 real images, the synthetic models lagged significantly in recall. They struggled to detect sea urchins situated far from the camera that were heavily obscured by haze, falling short of the sensitivity achieved by models trained on real data.

captions.F4: Qualitative comparison of sea urchin detection on real-world marine images from SeaClear. Top row: ground truth (GT); middle row: predictions from DETR trained on synthetic data ($5\times$ size); bottom row: predictions from DETR trained on real data. While the synthetic-trained model accurately captures clear foreground urchins, it tends to miss heavily hazed urchins in the background.

sections.heading: Why does adding more data fail to help? Three key bottlenecks revealed
sections.summary: This section identifies three core barriers in synthetic-to-real transfer: visual fidelity, scene diversity, and the lack of comprehensive generalization benchmarks. It outlines future technical improvements required for underwater simulators.
sections.details:
The performance plateau observed when scaling up synthetic data indicates that the bottleneck lies not in dataset size, but in data fidelity and diversity.

- **Oversimplified optical modeling**: While the deferred-shading haze model is fast, it cannot capture spatially heterogeneous, view-dependent light transport. Crucial underwater phenomena like caustics (focused light patterns from surface waves), suspended particles, and marine snow are absent, widening the sim-to-real gap under heavily degraded conditions.
- **Limited scene and asset diversity**: With only 5 sea urchin meshes and 30 terrain variants, generating thousands of images failed to broaden the distribution of underlying geometries and textures. Truly scalable automatic asset generation is necessary to prevent structural saturation.
- **Difficulty of benchmarking generalization**: The SeaClear test set was collected at a single marine site, lacking environmental variety. The high score of the real-data baseline may simply reflect identical imaging conditions between training and test sets. Building comprehensive marine perception benchmarks covering diverse geographical regions and water depths is an urgent need for the community.

sections.heading: Looking ahead: What synthetic data means for the future of underwater robotics
sections.summary: Although closing the entire real-world domain gap remains an open challenge, the work proves that zero-shot object detection using purely synthetic data is viable. Advancing light transport models and standardizing diverse benchmarks are key to scaling marine perception.
sections.details:
This work extended IsaacSim-based OceanSim to provide a highly configurable underwater synthetic data generation pipeline and a ROS2 wrapper. By reconstructing 3D assets from a few real images and applying domain randomization alongside optical haze in simulation, the authors successfully trained models capable of zero-shot sea urchin detection in the real ocean.

While a gap in recall remains compared to real-data baselines, this challenge can be addressed through improved physical light transport formulations and automated asset generation. The authors have open-sourced their code (https://github.com/umfieldrobotics/OceanSim), providing a solid foundation for large-scale marine perception learning.

takeaways: Object detection models trained entirely on simulated synthetic data can achieve viable zero-shot performance on real-world marine imagery.

Different model architectures benefit from different randomization aspects: CNNs (YOLO) gain heavily from pixel appearance (haze), whereas Transformers (DETR) rely more on structural diversity (terrain).
Simply increasing the number of synthetic images does not solve sim-to-real gaps; asset diversity and the physical fidelity of light transport simulation are fundamentally essential.
Advancing marine perception requires not only better simulators, but also diverse real-world benchmarks covering multiple geographic sites and depths.
limitations: The deferred shading underwater optical model is computationally fast, but omits caustics, marine snow, and spatially varying light scattering.
The limited pool of base 3D assets (5 sea urchins, 30 terrains) causes structural scene diversity to saturate even when scaling dataset size.
The real-world evaluation dataset (SeaClear) is limited to a single marine site, leaving generalization to other regions or extreme turbidity untested.
